reading_plan: Source title: Multi-criteria thermoeconomic and thermodynamic assessments of the desalination-integrated two-phase liquid-immersion data center cooling system. Source type: peer_reviewed_paper. The first visual look shows an 18-page journal research article, with a Summary, dense two-column technical prose, numbered equations, a system schematic, a calculation flowchart, three tables, multiple performance plots, nomenclature, 47 references, and three coefficient appendices. I will follow its printed order in roughly paragraph-to-page steps, staying toward shorter stretches where assumptions, transport equations, or cost definitions accumulate and taking longer stretches through documentary lists. Claims will be recorded as encountered, with subsequent restatements identified as moves rather than duplicated as new findings. Readings from figures, tables, and rendered equations will be named and marked paraphrased; uncertainty or differing printed values will remain visible. Citation numbers will retain the printed grouping or bracket style, with one matching source-internal reference entry per cited work; line wrapping and discretionary line-end hyphenation are normalized in the entries. The reading follows the authors’ argument and its stated scope without assessing whether it ultimately holds.

reading_path.location: PDF p. 1 / journal p. 10453, title and Summary
reading_path.moves: The title announces a multi-criteria engineering assessment. The Summary states the practical problem, proposes a hybrid system, identifies a research gap, and gives a compressed report of methods and findings. At this opening, these are announced results; their derivation is still ahead.

claims.text: Waste-heat management significantly affects energy-efficient data-center operation; the proposed desalination and data-center cooling hybrid aims to reduce the cost drawback of that waste heat.
Two-phase liquid-immersion cooling is promising for high heat-flux removal, but research on its waste-heat management is lacking.

The proposed design uses immersion-cooling waste heat to warm the feed of a direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) module; the study spans cooling loads of 0.7-1.5 kW and membrane areas of 5-75 cm².
The assessment combines thermodynamics, economics, and thermoeconomics through an exergy-cost matrix specific to the proposed design.
The maximum thermal and exergy efficiencies are found as 64.5% and 53.7%, respectively.
Daily distilled-water production can reach 6.13 kg at the highest cooling load and membrane area.
The hybrid has higher capital and operating costs than stand-alone cooling.
The authors interpret a 3.72-year payback period as showing economic feasibility for real applications.
The levelized product cost of the hybrid is reported as 2.69-5.33 SGD/h.
The Summary locates the best optimization trade-off at 1.1 kW and a membrane-area range of 5.12-5.19 cm².

reading_path.meaning: We begin with a proposed way to turn cooling waste heat into a water product. The opening treats physical performance, water output, and cost as joint reasons to investigate the design, without yet showing how they are calculated.

claims.text: The authors say a detailed understanding of this combined concept is missing and that waste-heat-utilization studies have usually concerned air-cooled systems; system-scale liquid-cooled studies have not been widely performed, as far as they know.
Liquid cooling can remove higher heat flux than air cooling because the working liquids have better heat-removal performance.
Indirect liquid cooling is more established but has leakage risks in circulating pipework and layouts sized for specific cooling loads.

Direct cooling uses dielectric liquids in contact with equipment, avoiding server- or rack-level liquid piping and allowing modification for different cooling loads; it includes jet impingement, spray cooling, and two-phase immersion.
Two-phase immersion gives a more uniform equipment-surface temperature through latent heat transfer, and direct methods can operate independently or with conventional air cooling.
